name: The Scorching Tempo

stars.name: Scorching Tempo A
stars.notes: Blazing blue main-sequence star only three million years old, somehow condensed from gas recaptured after an ancient supernova; its ultraviolet output sterilizes everything within forty AU.

stars.name: Scorching Tempo B
stars.notes: Yellow-white companion co-formed with the primary on a tight 2.1 AU orbit, contributing its own harsh glare to the inner inferno.

stars.name: Scorching Tempo C
stars.notes: Pulsar spinning once every 2.3 seconds on a 190 AU orbit, the collapsed corpse of the system's original sun; its beam sweeps the planetary plane like a metronome.

planets.name: Accelerando
planets.notes: Glassy innermost world whose surface was fused smooth by the young O star's ignition flash.

planets.name: Bravura
planets.notes: Radiation-kneaded lava world kept molten as much by flux as by its own interior.

planets.name: Coda
planets.notes: Airless rock veined with supernova-forged metals; lander telemetry ends abruptly whenever the pulsar beam crosses it.

planets.name: Da Capo
planets.notes: Wind-scoured dune world whose thin atmosphere condenses on the night side and boils away each dawn.

planets.name: Encore
planets.notes: Ringed colossus whose ring plane hosts the Ultramarine Debt; nine cratered moons keep perfect, suspiciously regular resonance.

planets.name: Fortissimo
planets.notes: Storm-banded giant emitting auroral screams whenever the pulsar beam grazes its magnetosphere.

planets.name: Glissando
planets.notes: Nitrogen-frosted ice world with cryovolcanic plumes aligned, oddly, toward the neutron companion.

planets.name: Hemiola
planets.notes: Dark sentinel of the outer halo, its surface dusted with material ejected from the primordial supernova.

anomalies.name: Ultramarine Debt
anomalies.location: orbit 5, threaded through Encore's ring plane
anomalies.notes: Catalogued causality fracture where instrument clocks disagree by fractions of a second and logged events occasionally precede their causes; the consortium maintains a standing ban on crewed approaches.

asteroid_belts.name: Pizzicato Band
asteroid_belts.notes: Metal-rich supernova ejecta condensed into a brilliant band; sampling drones return alloy data no forge can reproduce.

stations.name: Ledgerwatch Station
stations.location: distant halo, 300 AU from the barycenter
stations.notes: Fully automated observation platform with a skeleton rotation crew swapped out every quarter to limit radiation dosage.

faction_control.notes: Consortium charter grants exclusive access; escort cutters accompany every science vessel through the pulsar beam corridor.

history: The system was flagged when a deep survey matched an impossible blue star with a middle-aged pulsar, forcing theorists to accept a recent re-ignition from supernova-enriched gas.
Confirmation of the recapture model made The Scorching Tempo the most cited stellar laboratory of its generation.
After automated probes recorded effects preceding their causes near Encore, the Vantage Research Consortium closed the system and built Ledgerwatch Station to study the fracture from a safe remove.
description: Three mismatched suns rule this system: a newborn blue giant burning furiously beside its yellow-white second, while a thousand-year-old pulsar ticks across the outskirts like a wound metronome. Eight planets orbit far outside the killing zone, from the fused glass of Accelerando to the frosted halo world Hemiola. Everything that survives here survives by distance.

The Vantage Research Consortium keeps the only foothold, an automated platform parked three hundred AU out, and its light shuttle traffic is the sole sign of habitation in a system otherwise lethal to visit. Scientists prize the Pizzicato Band's impossible alloys and, above all, the Ultramarine Debt threading Encore's rings, where causality visibly frays. Civilian traffic is turned back at the beam corridor without exception.

Consortium logs hint that the fracture is widening by measurable increments, though no one will say what happens when it touches the ring shepherds. The pulsar's beam has begun arriving microseconds ahead of schedule, as if the whole system were accelerating toward some closing bar. Visitors willing to risk the corridor speak of hearing the tick twice, once outside and once inside their own skulls.
